title: لَا النَّافِيَة versus لَا النَّاهِيَة, and كَادَ — the Verb of Being About To
summary: Working the prohibition exercises, the class confronts the fact that لَا تَأْكُلُ and لَا تَأْكُلْ look almost identical on the page but mean opposite things: the first merely reports that you are not eating, the second forbids it, and the jazm is the only signal. The session's main new item is كَادَ, a فِعْل الْمُقَارَبَة meaning to be on the point of something, which must always be followed by a مُضَارِع verb — illustrated through five places it occurs in the Qur'ān.
key_points: لَا النَّافِيَة negates or reports — لِمَ لَا تَأْكُلُ يَا أَخِي, why are you not eating — and leaves the verb with its ḍamma. لَا النَّاهِيَة forbids — لَا تَأْكُلْ هَذَا, do not eat this — and puts the verb in jazm with a sukūn.
The two differ only by that final vowel on the page, so meaning and the sukūn together are what distinguish them. The teacher offered an Urdu memory hook: نَهِي carries the sense of no, don't.
النَّافِيَة is not restricted to questions; it can be a plain statement, such as saying that someone is not going to the airport today.
كَادَ، يَكَادُ is a فِعْل الْمُقَارَبَة (fiʿl al-muqārabah : verb of proximity), from قَرِيب, meaning to be about to do something — أَكَادُ أَصِلُ إِلَى الْمَسْجِدِ, I am about to reach the masjid.
كَادَ conjugates across the same persons as any مَاضِي — كَادَ، كَادَا، كَادُوا، كَادَتْ، كِدْتَ، كِدْتُ، كِدْنَ — and it also has the مُضَارِع form يَكَادُ.
The rule that matters: كَادَ must be followed by a مُضَارِع verb naming what was nearly done — كَادُوا يَقْتُلُونَنِي، يَكَادُ الْبَرْقُ يَخْطَفُ، يَكَادُ الْجَرَسُ يَرِنُّ.

The wāw of the masculine plural goes silent when the word is connected to what follows, much like هَمْزَة الْوَصْل; it is pronounced when a hamza follows, as in أَلَّا تَعْبُدُوا إِلَّا إِيَّاهُ, but swallowed before the حُرُوف شَمْسِيَّة.
Two hamzas in a row are intolerable, so أَنَا with أَكَلَ gives آكُلُ rather than أَأْكُلُ, and likewise آخُذُ. The underlying verb is still أَكَلَ, the same root as كُلْ.

There is an exception to the negation rule: مَا can negate a مُضَارِع verb, but only for the حَال — what is happening right now. أَنَا مَا أَشْرَبُ الْقَهْوَةَ الْآنَ means I am not drinking coffee at this moment, whereas لَا أَشْرَبُ الْقَهْوَةَ denies the habit. مَا cannot carry a future sense here, and the teacher noted it is rare enough that no Qur'ānic instance came to mind.
فِعْل التَّعَجُّب can take an attached pronoun instead of naming the thing: مَا أَطْوَلَهُ (how tall he is), مَا أَكْثَرَهُمْ (how many they are).
فِي أَثْنَاء means during or in the middle of, and is مُضَاف to what follows: فِي أَثْنَاءِ الدَّرْسِ، فِي أَثْنَاءِ الصَّلَاةِ.
نَظَّارَة (glasses) comes from نَظَرَ, to look — the instrument through which one looks.

Vocabulary: كَنَسَ، يَكْنُسُ (to sweep) with its مِكْنَسَة, نَعَسَ (to doze) beside نَامَ from نَوْم, بَكَى، يَبْكِي (to cry), جَرَس (bell) with رَنَّ، يَرِنُّ (to ring), بَرْق (lightning), خَطَفَ (to snatch away), سَطَا (to attack or harm), رَكَنَ (to incline toward), اِنْقَلَبَ (to flip over), تَأَمَّلْ (ponder), and مَا يَلِي (what follows).
questions: [00:02:00] Q: Why does the wāw seem to disappear when reading? — A: Like هَمْزَة الْوَصْل, it goes silent mid-phrase; it surfaces before a hamza, as in أَلَّا تَعْبُدُوا إِلَّا إِيَّاهُ, but not before the حُرُوف شَمْسِيَّة.

[00:11:00] Q: What is the difference between لَا النَّافِيَة and لَا النَّاهِيَة? — A: النَّافِيَة informs that something is not happening; النَّاهِيَة forbids it. The prohibition carries the jazm, so لَا تَأْكُلُ against لَا تَأْكُلْ.
[00:13:00] Q: Is the negating لَا always in a question? — A: No, it can be any statement; the exercise simply happened to use questions.
[00:16:00] Q: Why is it آكُلُ and not أَأْكُلُ? — A: Two hamzas in a row are hard to pronounce, so they merge; the root verb is still أَكَلَ.
[00:17:00] Q: Is the original verb أَكَلَ? — A: Yes — the same root behind the command كُلْ.
[00:29:10] Q: What does نَظَّارَة mean? — A: Glasses — from نَظَرَ, to look, so the tool one looks through.

[00:35:00] Q: If you leave out الْآنَ, does مَا make it past? — A: No. The verb is still مُضَارِع, so it is automatically understood as the present moment, since مَا with a مُضَارِع can only carry that sense.
[00:32:00] Q: What does اِبْكِ mean? — A: It is the command cry — usable sarcastically, as in cry about it.
[00:38:21] Q: What was the exclamation construction called again? — A: فِعْل التَّعَجُّب, as in مَا أَطْوَلَ حَامِدًا, how tall Ḥāmid is.

quiz.q: What is the only written difference between لَا تَأْكُلُ and لَا تَأْكُلْ?
options: The ending: a ḍamma for the statement, a sukūn for the prohibition
quiz.a: The jazm is the whole signal — لَا تَأْكُلُ reports that you are not eating, لَا تَأْكُلْ forbids it.

quiz.q: Which لَا is being used in لِمَ لَا تَأْكُلُ يَا أَخِي?
quiz.a: It asks why you are not eating, which is information rather than prohibition — hence no jazm.

quiz.q: What does كَادَ mean, and what is it classed as?
options: It was — one of كَانَ's sisters
To be about to — a فِعْل الْمُقَارَبَة
To become — a verb of transformation
quiz.a: From the sense of قَرِيب, nearness: being on the point of doing something.
Every example given bears this out: كَادُوا يَقْتُلُونَنِي، يَكَادُ الْبَرْقُ يَخْطَفُ، يَكَادُ الْجَرَسُ يَرِنُّ.

quiz.q: Why is it أَنَا آكُلُ rather than أَنَا أَأْكُلُ?
options: Because two hamzas in a row are merged for ease of pronunciation
Because the first person drops its prefix
Because the verb is a مَصْدَر
quiz.a: The same instinct behind كُلْ and خُذْ: Arabic avoids the awkward sequence.

quiz.q: When may مَا be used to negate a مُضَارِع verb?
options: Only when the meaning is the present moment, the حَال
quiz.a: مَا أَشْرَبُ الْقَهْوَةَ الْآنَ is I am not drinking coffee right now; it cannot carry a future meaning.

quiz.q: What is the difference between لَا أَشْرَبُ الْقَهْوَةَ and مَا أَشْرَبُ الْقَهْوَةَ الْآنَ?
options: The first denies the habit; the second denies it at this moment
The first is future; the second is past
quiz.a: لَا negates generally, while مَا here pins the denial to right now.

quiz.q: What does فِي أَثْنَاء mean, and how does it behave?
options: During — it is مُضَاف to the following word
Because of — it takes a verb
quiz.a: فِي أَثْنَاءِ الدَّرْسِ, during the lesson — the following noun takes a kasra as the مُضَاف إِلَيْهِ.

quiz.q: How can فِعْل التَّعَجُّب be shortened when the thing is already known?
options: By attaching a pronoun — مَا أَطْوَلَهُ
quiz.a: مَا أَطْوَلَهُ means how tall he is, and مَا أَكْثَرَهُمْ how many they are.

quiz.q: What does نَظَّارَة mean and where does it come from?
options: Glasses, from نَظَرَ — the tool one looks through
quiz.a: The teacher built it from نَظَرَ, to look, on the pattern of an instrument.

quran_examples.arabic: وَقَضَىٰ رَبُّكَ أَلَّا تَعْبُدُوا إِلَّا إِيَّاهُ
quran_examples.transliteration: wa-qaḍā rabbuka allā taʿbudū illā iyyāh
quran_examples.translation: And your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him.
quran_examples.note: Used to show when the wāw of the plural is actually pronounced: it surfaces here because a hamza follows, where before a شَمْسِيَّة letter it would go silent.

quran_examples.translation: Indeed, the people overpowered me and were about to kill me.
quran_examples.note: Hārūn عَلَيْهِ السَّلَام answering Mūsā عَلَيْهِ السَّلَام after the calf. The clearest example of كَادَ: the plural كَادُوا followed by the مُضَارِع يَقْتُلُونَنِي, and اسْتَضْعَفُونِي from ضَعِيف, they saw me as weak.

quran_examples.translation: The lightning almost snatches away their sight.
quran_examples.note: A student's answer: يَكَادُ with the مُضَارِع يَخْطَفُ, conveying that the flash was so bright it was on the point of taking their vision.

quran_examples.arabic: وَلَوْلَا أَن ثَبَّتْنَاكَ لَقَدْ كِدتَّ تَرْكَنُ إِلَيْهِمْ شَيْئًا قَلِيلًا
quran_examples.transliteration: wa-lawlā an thabbatnāka la-qad kidta tarkanu ilayhim shayʾan qalīlā
quran_examples.translation: And if We had not strengthened you, you would have nearly inclined to them a little.
quran_examples.note: The second-person form كِدْتَ, addressed to the Prophet ﷺ, followed by تَرْكَنُ from رَكَنَ، يَرْكُنُ, to incline toward.

quran_examples.arabic: يَكَادُونَ يَسْطُونَ بِالَّذِينَ يَتْلُونَ عَلَيْهِمْ آيَاتِنَا
quran_examples.transliteration: yakādūna yasṭūna bi-lladhīna yatlūna ʿalayhim āyātinā
quran_examples.translation: They are nearly assaulting those who recite to them Our verses.
quran_examples.note: The مُضَارِع plural يَكَادُونَ, which the teacher noted is the less common form; سَطَا means to attack or harm.

quran_examples.arabic: يَكَادُ زَيْتُهَا يُضِيءُ وَلَوْ لَمْ تَمْسَسْهُ نَارٌ
quran_examples.transliteration: yakādu zaytuhā yuḍīʾu wa-law lam tamsas-hu nār
quran_examples.translation: Its oil almost gives light, even if untouched by fire.
quran_examples.note: From the Āyat al-Nūr, offered by a student: the oil is so pure it is on the point of shining of itself — يَكَادُ again followed by a مُضَارِع.
